content: A 21-year-old male with a history of sickle cell anemia experienced recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever starting at the age of 14. By the time he was 16, he had developed both mitral valve insufficiency and stenosis. While on prophylactic antibiotics, he remained free of rheumatic fever recurrences until three weeks prior to his final hospital admission. At that time, he developed an upper respiratory infection, which was followed by the onset of acute migratory polyarthritis. This condition rapidly progressed, leading to severe cardiac dysfunction and ultimately his death. At autopsy, the heart was found to be significantly enlarged, weighing 675 grams, with notable enlargement of the left atrium. Both the aortic and mitral valves exhibited fibrosis and the presence of small, fresh verrucae, which are characteristic of acute rheumatic fever. A gross photograph of the mitral valve revealed pronounced thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflet. These verrucae appeared as irregular, warty projections at sites of erosion on the inflamed endocardial surface. They are thought to result from fibrin deposition at points where the valve leaflets come into contact. A low-power photomicrograph of the heart tissue showed a relatively normal appearance at this magnification. However, a higher-power photomicrograph of the myocardium revealed the presence of Aschoff bodies within the interstitial tissue, particularly around blood vessels. These Aschoff bodies are hallmark lesions of acute rheumatic fever. A detailed high-power photomicrograph of the myocardium demonstrated the cellular composition of an Aschoff body. These lesions consist of a central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, occasional plasma cells, and activated histiocytes known as Anitschkow cells or Aschoff cells. These distinctive histiocytes have abundant amphophilic cytoplasm and nuclei with a central, wavy chromatin pattern resembling a caterpillar, hence the term caterpillar cells. Another high-power photomicrograph of the myocardium showed an Aschoff body containing a multinucleated Aschoff giant cell, further highlighting the pathological changes associated with acute rheumatic fever.
